name: GripMCP – MCP Server for WordPress: Connect Claude & AI Assistants
author: Akshay T.

sections.description:
GripMCP turns your WordPress site into a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. Paste one address into your AI assistant, approve the connection, and you can manage your site’s content with AI in plain language: write and edit posts, upload images, organise categories and menus, moderate comments, look into errors, and more. Paid plans add more tools for developers, agencies and stores.

The assistant never gets more power than the person who connected it. Every action is checked against that WordPress user’s real role and capabilities, deletions wait for your approval unless you choose otherwise, and the endpoint stays off until you switch it on.

Connect in a minute

  • One address. Your site answers at its own address followed by /mcp.
  • One-click connect. In Claude, add a custom connector, paste the address, sign in to WordPress and approve. No tokens or config files. This uses the standard MCP authorization flow (OAuth 2.1 with PKCE and dynamic client registration), so other MCP clients that support it connect the same way.
  • Access tokens for config-file clients such as Claude Desktop or mcp-remote. Make as many as you need: tokens are stored hashed, expire after 90 days unless you choose otherwise, work only at the GripMCP endpoint, and can be revoked at any time. WordPress Application Passwords work too.
  • You choose who can connect. Administrators always can; other roles only when you allow them.

What your assistant can do with the free plugin

  • Content: list, read, create, update, edit in place and delete posts, pages and custom post types; categories, tags and custom taxonomies; menus; comments; custom fields; reading WordPress’s settings (changing them stays with you, in Settings); revisions and restore.
  • Media: upload from a link or a file in the chat, place images into a post or set them as the featured image. On assistants that support in-chat panels, you can drag images onto an upload panel right in the conversation, or open an upload page when the chat cannot reach your site.
  • Users: list users and their roles.
  • Safety: deletions held for your approval, with a check of what they would break; revisions to undo an edit.
  • Site health: site health checks, the PHP error log, a record of recent crashes, cron events, cache flushing (including Elementor and page-cache plugins such as LiteSpeed Cache and WP Rocket), and a check of how any page renders.
  • Plugin abilities: on WordPress 6.9 and later, discover and run the read-only actions other plugins publish for AI clients through the WordPress Abilities API, such as looking up orders, products or form entries. Actions that change something stay on the plugin’s own screens.
  • Progress cards: for requests that take several steps, one live card in the chat with each step and the outcome.

With a paid plan

GripMCP Creator, Operator and Fleet are a separate plugin with more tools for developers, agencies and stores, sold at gripmcp.com and not hosted on WordPress.org. Each plan includes the ones before it; the pricing page compares them.

The Abilities tools appear on WordPress 6.9 and later. If tools are added after you connect, for example by a WordPress update, reconnect GripMCP in your AI app to load them; GripMCP tells the assistant.

Safe by default

  • The endpoint is off until you switch it on, and it requires HTTPS.
  • Every tool checks the connected user’s WordPress capabilities. GripMCP never grants a capability the user does not already have.
  • The assistant writes content, not code: a change that would add code such as a script, an embedded frame, an event handler, a javascript: link or a block’s custom CSS to a post or custom field is refused with the reason, even for an administrator. Code already on your pages is kept as it is, and you can add code yourself in the WordPress editor.
  • Access keys work only on the GripMCP endpoint, not on the rest of the WordPress API.
  • Destructive actions (deleting posts, pages, media, comments, categories, tags and menus, replacing a menu’s items, and removing a page-builder layout) are set to “Ask me first” on a new install: each one waits for you to approve it on a page in your own WordPress admin. Requests waiting for you are also listed on the Approvals tab of the GripMCP screen, with a count on its menu item, so a lost link never strands one. There is no way for an assistant to approve its own request. Under Permissions you can switch them off entirely, or allow them without asking.
  • Before a destructive action is put up for approval, GripMCP checks what it would break: a page that is your homepage or in a menu, an image used as the logo, site icon or a featured image, a category that is the default one or still in use. You see the findings with the request; high-risk ones recommend trying it on a staging copy first and ask you to confirm before it runs.
  • Credentials are protected: secret-looking options are refused, and passwords and API keys inside other plugins’ settings (a payment gateway’s secret key, an SMTP password) are shown to the assistant as “[redacted]”.
  • A per-user rate limit, an activity log of your assistant’s tool calls, and a connection diagnostics log for when a connector stops working.

In-chat progress cards

For requests that take several steps, assistants that support in-chat panels (the MCP Apps standard) show one live card with each step and its result, then the outcome. An assistant that declares the extensions it supports when it connects, and leaves panels out of them, is not sent the card tools at all. Developers can switch off the upload panel with the gripmcp/in_chat_uploads filter, and the cards with the gripmcp/progress_cards filter.

External services

GripMCP contacts other servers only in these cases:

  • Freemius (freemius.com), which sells and licenses the paid plans and, if you opt in, collects usage data for GripMCP. After activation GripMCP asks whether you want to opt in; skipping it sends nothing. If you opt in, Freemius receives your name and email, your site’s address, title and language, your WordPress, PHP and GripMCP versions, whether GripMCP is active or uninstalled, and the list of your plugins and themes (you can untick this one on the opt-in screen), and GripMCP checks in with Freemius once a day while you stay opted in. Freemius is also contacted when you open the Upgrade page (it loads prices and the checkout, with no details about your site), buy a plan or activate a licence, or send the optional feedback form when you deactivate (anonymous by default). The Upgrade page also loads Google’s analytics script (privacy), which records nothing because GripMCP offers no trial. See GripMCP’s privacy policy and terms.
  • WordPress.org (api.wordpress.org): Site Health’s update check, the same request WordPress itself sends. Privacy policy.
  • A web address you or your assistant give, to download a file into the Media Library.
  • Your own site, to load a page for the page-render check.
sections.installation:
1. Upload the gripmcp folder to /wp-content/plugins/, or go to Plugins → Add New → Upload Plugin and choose the zip.
  2. Activate GripMCP.
  3. Open GripMCP in the admin menu and switch the endpoint on with the switch at the top right. It saves as soon as you change it.
  4. Copy the endpoint address from the Setup tab.
  5. Connect your assistant:
    • Claude (web, desktop or mobile): Settings → Connectors → Add custom connector, paste the address, then sign in to WordPress and approve.
    • Config-file clients: create a token under Access and use it as Authorization: Bearer <token>.
  6. Choose what the assistant may do under Permissions.

The short /mcp address needs pretty permalinks (Settings → Permalinks set to anything but “Plain”). Without them the Setup tab shows the longer REST address instead, ending in ?rest_route=/gripmcp/v1/rpc, which works with any permalink setting.
sections.faq:
Which assistants work with GripMCP?

Any MCP client that supports the Streamable HTTP transport. Claude connects with one click through a custom connector. Clients that read a config file connect with an access token.

Is it safe?

Every tool call runs as a WordPress user and is checked against that user’s capabilities, exactly as wp-admin would check them. For the tightest control, connect as a dedicated user with a limited role, and keep “Destructive actions” on “Ask me first” (the default) or set it to “Off”.

Does it send my data anywhere?

Only if you choose to. Usage data goes to Freemius only if you opt in after activation, and Freemius is otherwise contacted only when you open the Upgrade page, buy a plan or send deactivation feedback. The other services listed under “External services” are contacted only when your assistant asks for that action.

What is in the free plugin, and what do the paid plans add?

The free plugin (the Explorer plan) covers everyday site care: content, media, categories, menus, comments, custom fields, the list of users, reading WordPress’s settings, revisions, approvals for deletes, the debug log, site health and read-only plugin abilities. No plan limits access tokens or connected apps. The paid plans are a separate plugin with more tools for developers, agencies and stores, sold at gripmcp.com, where the pricing page compares them. Each paid licence covers a set number of sites.

How do I move from a paid plan back to the free plugin?

You don’t have to: when a licence ends, the paid version keeps running with the free plugin’s features. To switch to this free plugin, for its updates from WordPress.org, install and activate it first (if WordPress offers to replace the copy you have, accept), and only then delete the paid copy if it is still listed. Your settings, connected apps and activity log carry over. Deleting GripMCP while no other copy is installed removes all of them, and your assistant then has to connect again; your site’s content is never touched.

What does it store on my site?

Its settings, hashed access tokens, OAuth clients and tokens, an activity log of tool calls (time, tool, user, result, duration and IP address: kept 3 days on the free plan, 7 on Creator and 90 on Operator and Fleet, and up to 30 days longer after a licence lapses), a connection log, page-builder restore points, approval requests while they wait, the progress cards’ steps (kept 7 days), images uploaded through the chat until they are added (2 hours at most), and a short list of recent PHP fatal errors. Deleting the plugin from the Plugins screen removes all of it.

Does it require HTTPS?

Yes, by default. On a site that is not served over HTTPS, the Setup tab shows a “Require HTTPS” switch you can turn off for testing, but tokens sent over plain HTTP can be intercepted.

One-click connect does not work. What should I check?

Open GripMCP → Activity → Connection diagnostics. It lists every token issued and every refused request with the reason. One-click connect needs HTTPS and a site at the root of its domain, because the discovery documents must sit at /.well-known/. If a security plugin blocks .well-known paths, allow them. Sites in a subdirectory can connect with an access token instead.

My host strips the Authorization header.

Some Apache and LiteSpeed setups drop it before PHP sees it, and then every app is refused. When you open the GripMCP screen, your browser sends the site a test request with the header, the way WordPress’s own Site Health checks it, and the Setup tab warns you if it does not get through. To fix it, add this to the very top of .htaccess:

RewriteEngine On
RewriteCond %{HTTP:Authorization} ^(.*)
RewriteRule ^(.*) - [E=HTTP_AUTHORIZATION:%1]

My site already uses the /mcp address.

Change GripMCP’s short address by adding define( 'GRIPMCP_SHORT_PATH', 'ai' ); to wp-config.php (any single word works), or set it to an empty string to turn the short address off and use the longer REST address. Then copy the new address from the Setup tab into your assistant.

How do I report a problem?

Open GripMCP → Activity → Report a problem and describe what you were trying to do and what happened. GripMCP writes a post around your description and adds what is needed to look into it: your WordPress, PHP and plugin versions, your GripMCP settings, what it noticed in its own logs, and the error lines from your site’s PHP error logs.

With the free plugin, support is on the GripMCP forum here on WordPress.org: click Copy post, then Open the forum, and paste it into a new topic with the title shown above it. Forum posts are public, so read it first and remove anything you would rather keep private; GripMCP leaves your site address out of it. On a paid plan, GripMCP writes an email instead: click Copy email, paste it into a new email to support@gripmcp.com with the subject shown above it, and send it, or download it as a file and attach it.

Settings that stop every app from connecting, such as a switched-off endpoint, are shown on the GripMCP screen next to their fix, so you may not need to write in at all. The report is written to leave out passwords, tokens, email and IP addresses, phone numbers, server folder names and your content, but read it before you send it. The plugin never sends it: only you do.

Which versions of WordPress and PHP does it support?

WordPress 6.2 or later, tested up to 7.1. PHP 7.4 or later, tested up to 8.5.
